title: Chapter 5: Old Brass, Freely Given
blurb: The order Ravi handed back has come back worse, and the only fix he can find is metal that has to be given freely.

blocks.text: At two in the morning, seven days to the hour since I'd signed for it, WO-5-002 rewrote itself while I watched.

I was in the office because it was the only room where I could think, with Dusty on the cold patch of floor by the door and the Works Book open under the lamp. The office clock clicked onto the hour. The red lines at the bottom of the entry went soft, the way ink does while it's still wet, and came back different.

``` WO-5-002.   FLOOR 5.   TIER 1. HELD BY:          THE CARETAKER. RETURNED ON DISPUTE. GRADE REQUIRED:   2. SYMPTOM:          WET CHILL. WATERY COUGH. WORSENED. STATUS:           OPEN. ESCALATED x1. ```

The cough arrived about a second after the word did. It came up from somewhere under my ribs, low and wet and doubled, and folded me over the desk, and when it was finished I had my forehead on the blotter and the taste of pipe water at the back of my throat.

"Sorry," I said to the riser, which was five floors up and couldn't hear me. "I'm sorry. I've had you on a slip for a week. I handed you to somebody else and got you handed back, and none of that is a repair. You're getting a proper one. Not another slip on another party. A proper repair. I promise."
Then I sat up and looked at the 2 and understood that I had no idea where grade-two anything came from.

Dusty got up when I did. He does that. In the lift he leant his back against my shins, and I pressed the lit button with the side of my fist, because my fingers had stopped bending at the ruling and hadn't started again. My knuckles had gone. My hands were hot and tight and shiny, like something left to prove.
The doors opened on floor 5, on the green baize board by the lift, and the Felt's complaint was still pinned to it. The grey letters had spread since half twelve. They looked furry now.
"It went up," I said.

"I heard you," said Walter. He'd walked out ahead of me and stood on the brown lino, a scruffy grey lurcher with a working man's voice coming out of him, which I am still not used to. "Whole building heard you."
"It wants grade two. I've got a box of joints under the desk from Ropewalk Lane. Good ones. Proper cast, I checked the—"
"New," Walter said.
"Brand new. Receipt and everything."
"New's grade one, son. Always. Don't matter what you paid or whose name's cast in it."
I coughed into my elbow for a while. When I came back up he was already walking, so I followed, which is how most of our conversations go.
"Then what's two?"
"Find metal that's been used every day in a house somebody lives in," he said. "Years of it. About as many years as you've been alive, for two. And get it given you. Don't take it. Given."

Riser 2's cupboard was where I'd left it. I opened it with the heels of both hands. The joints were weeping harder than they had at midnight. The wet had come down the iron in a sheet and darkened the bottom of the door, and the bites in the caulking looked deeper in the torchlight, or I was more frightened of them. The nest at the foot of the pipe was quiet. Mrs Quarry's brass fish was still on the rim where I'd promised to leave it.

"I could serve it," I said. "Couldn't I. The Felt. It's back on me, and you told me I could put it on the deeper one, and there isn't anything deeper. Under the Felt there's only the slab, and the slab's just old."
Walter sat down on the lino. "Look at the pipe, son."
So I looked at the pipe.

What it wanted was somebody to cut out the bad and make the joints again. That's all a leak ever wants. And the Felt is a mould. A clever one, a head tenant with opinions about light, but it hasn't got hands or a hacksaw or a box of anything. If I served it, the cough would go into the grey and stay there, and the order would sit open on the Felt the way it had sat on me, getting a grade worse every week, and the floor would never get clear of it. Walter had told me what orders do when they're left to get worse. They come through. Under this cupboard there was a landing on the fourth floor, and a cupboard on that landing, and a kitchen wall not far from it.

Then there was the serving itself. To put a slip into the Felt's possession I'd have had to put it into the Felt's home, through the panel it had filed against me for opening. And it had been here a great deal longer than me. Mrs Wrobel had told me how a tie goes. The one with more standing wins it.
"No," I said. "It doesn't want a slip. It wants a plumber."
"Then go and be one," said Walter, and lay down with his chin on his paws.
"Hear that?" I told the riser. "Plumber. Hang on."

I didn't sleep. At eight I was on the fourth-floor landing with riser 2's cupboard open, because if the run upstairs was weeping harder I wanted to know how much was getting down. The tidemark on the back wall had climbed past where I'd pencilled it. The brick under it was dark and cold to the back of my hand.
I was talking to it. I do that.

"Old brass," I said. "Old brass somebody uses every day and would actually give me. And not the lobby's, because if I start unscrewing the lobby the association will have me on the bins for the rest of my natural life. So where am I meant to—"
Behind me, 4C's door opened.

Mrs Wrobel stood there in a grey cardigan with the Yale on its string round her neck. Behind her, inside the door, Jurek's brown coat hung over his slippers the way it always did, as if he'd just stepped out of both.
"You are coughing on my landing again, Mr Caretaker."
"Sorry. It's the riser. The one from the other night. It's got worse and I need—"
"I heard what you need." She looked at the open cupboard, then at my hands, for longer. Then she went back in and left the door open, which I took to mean come in, and which it did.

Her kitchen was small and very clean, with one window onto the yard and the extractor I'd promised to look at ticking in the wall. Over the sink, on the tiles, was a brass bib tap with a cross head. Not chrome over brass. Brass all through, the cross head worn pale and soft where hands had turned it.

"Sixty years, that tap," Mrs Wrobel said. "Before us, and then us. Every day. Every cup of tea." She put her hand on it, briefly, the way you'd touch someone's shoulder going past. "You need old brass. Here is old brass. I give it to you."
She said *give* carefully, the way you set down a cup that's too full.
"On a condition," she went on. "You fit me a new one before you go. Today. I am seventy-one. I do not wash cups in the bath."

What I meant to say was thank you. What I said was, "That's a three-quarter bib. Look at the casting on it. That's proper yellow brass, that is, there's no pink in it, there's no pitting at all, and they put that bit of lead in back then so it cuts like butter. The thread on the tail'll be the old pattern. I'll want to clean it up before I—"
"Yes," said Mrs Wrobel. "It is very good brass. Sit. You eat first."

I always accept food. She fried me cold pierogi in butter and put them in front of me with a fork, and when the fork wouldn't stay in my fingers she took it off me and gave me a spoon instead, without comment, and I ate them with the spoon.
I bought her tap at Ropewalk Lane when they opened at nine, a plain chrome bib with a ceramic cartridge, with the money I'd been keeping back for the gas. Then I came back up and did the job.

It should have taken ten minutes. It took forty. I turned off her stopcock under the sink with the heel of my hand. I couldn't close my fingers round the spanner, so I worked it with both palms flat, like praying, a quarter-turn at a time, and the old tap gave with a long, tired creak, as if it had been waiting for somebody to ask.
Mrs Wrobel didn't offer to help. I'd have said no, and she knew it. She stood by the door with her arms folded, near the coat, and watched the old tap come off the wall, and didn't say a word.

I wrapped the new tail in tape, fed it in, and brought it up tight with my palms. I opened her stopcock. I turned the new tap on, and water came out, clean and straight, and didn't come out anywhere else.
She filled the kettle from it. "Good," she said. "Go."
I went down to the office with Jurek's tap wrapped in a tea towel she'd made me take.

The book only works in the office. Anything I want to tell it, I tell it there. I wrote under my old cause line, slowly, with the pen jammed in my fist like a child's crayon: *Felt grown through upper-run joints in the void, pushing sockets apart. Drove the key-eaters down to the slab, where they gnawed the joints.* That was the true shape of it, as far as I knew. Under it, where a party's name goes, I left the line empty.

Then I put the tap in the vice in the storeroom and took it apart. The headgear came off with a lot of persuading. Under it, in the seat, the washer was brass too, a little jumper worn bright on its face from sixty years of being pressed shut, and I put that in my shirt pocket, because you don't throw away a part that good. I sawed off the spout. What was left was a thick brass body with a threaded tail, heavy as a doorstop, and once I'd drifted the seat out of it and dressed both ends it was the shape of what I needed. A sleeve. Something to bridge the worst joint where the teeth had gone deepest, with nothing in it for teeth or threads to get into.
Dusty rode up with me. He didn't speak. He sat by the lift and watched me walk to the far end, coughing.

At riser 2 I drained down the run and talked the whole time. I told the riser what I was doing before I did it. I told it I was sorry about the hacksaw. I told the nest at the foot of the pipe I wasn't going anywhere near it, and I didn't. I cut out the bitten length above it, cleaned the iron back to bright, and offered up Jurek's brass.
That was when I felt it.

It was heavier. Not in my arm, where weight goes. In my hand. Downstairs in the vice it had been a heavy tap. Here, held against the pipe it was meant for, it was heavier than brass should be, the way a kettle is heavier than you thought when somebody's filled it without telling you. My fat, useless fingers knew it before I did. I stood there holding it, with the run dripping on my boots, and thought: oh. So that's what two feels like. Or three. More than the pipe needs, anyway. Enough.
It went on sweet. I made both ends good and packed them and brought the whole thing up with my palms, and opened the valve, and watched.
Nothing wept. The iron above and below went from wet to damp to dry in front of me, and the sound in the cupboard changed from a drip to nothing, which is the best sound a cupboard can make.

I laid the order's carbon slip, which I'd brought up from the office, flat on the cupboard door, and signed the SIGNED OFF AT FAULT line with the pen in my fist. My name looked like it had been written on a bus.

The cough went out of my chest the way a tide goes out. One breath I was full of cold water. The next I wasn't. My hands stayed swollen and stiff, but I could feel the edge of a finger again, and then another, and when I made a fist it nearly closed.
"There," I told riser 2. "Proper job. Told you."
Back in the office the entry had gone black, every line of it, and the top of the page had changed too.
``` CARETAKER:   R. ANAND GRADE:       0 CREDITS:     4 HOLDING:     WO-5-003 CERTIFIED:   NONE ```
I read it twice. I always do. It didn't say well done, but I hadn't expected it to.
At four that afternoon the front door rubbed its frame on the dropped hinge and Imogen Tarrant came into the lobby with a surveyor behind her.
She had two coffees again. She gave me one and noticed my hands while she did it, and her face did something kind and quick and then put itself away.

"Courtesy visit," she said. "Not the city's inspection. Ours. So nothing we find counts, Ravi, and everything we don't find is good news for you. Two ways this goes. You walk us round, or we go away and come back with a date."
"I'll walk you round."

The surveyor was about the age I'd been at Fennick. He had a lanyard, a laser measure, a moisture meter and a clipboard he held like a shield. I watched him work and knew every move before he made it, and kept my hands in my jacket pockets, where nobody could see how little they'd hold.

We did all four floors. He measured, he tapped, he put his meter on walls. On the first floor he found an old brown stain on the landing ceiling and photographed it, and I told him it was a bath that overflowed years before my time, which it was, and he checked it with his meter and wrote down dry. On the fourth floor Lou Mabbott opened 4D with flour on her forearms and let him put his meter on the kitchen wall where the water had come through on my first night.
"Dry," he said.
"He did the roof," Lou told Imogen, nodding at me. "Middle of the night. Didn't even wake Danny."
"Did he," said Imogen, and looked at me over her coffee.
4C's door stayed shut. Behind it, Mrs Wrobel coughed once. Dry.

On the way down the surveyor stopped in the lobby to look at the front door's top hinge, wrote *door* on his clipboard, and underlined it. He hadn't found anything else. I'd known he wouldn't. There wasn't anything on the public floors to find, and I'd been surveying long enough to know what a clean walk-round feels like.
"Last thing," Imogen said. "The service lift. Just so we've seen it."
My first thought was no. My second was that saying no to a surveyor about a lift is the fastest way to get him to write *lift* on his clipboard and underline it twice.

And I had a theory about the lift, which I'd had plenty of nights to think through. The buttons above four answered to me. Mrs Wrobel had ridden up, but she'd ridden with me. Kit had stood at those doors with a parcel for the fifth floor and still had to ask me which way it was. Whatever lit that button lit it for the caretaker, the same way the book only took my name. Imogen would see a brass panel with painted-over holes, and a surveyor would see a lift certificate that wanted renewing, and that would be that.
Dusty lifted his head from the mat under the post table as we went past. He didn't get up.
Kit's parcel was still on the tiles by the service-lift doors. Imogen read the label as she passed it, the way you'd read a name badge, and didn't say anything.
I opened the doors with my key and the surveyor looked in at the cage and the panel and started writing.
"Aled," Imogen said, quite gently. "Would you wait in the van? Five minutes."

He went. She stepped into the lift. I stepped in after her, because it was my lift, and turned my key to show her the machine room was in the basement, and coughed, out of habit, though there was nothing left to cough.

She wasn't looking at the B. She was looking above the 4, at the lamp behind its glass bead, and she reached past my shoulder and pressed 5 with one finger, the way you'd press a doorbell at a house you'd been invited to.
It lit under her fingertip. Brighter, and warm, the way it lights for me.

The doors closed. The cage gave its little jolt and began to rise, and I stood there with my swollen hands in my pockets and Jurek's washer against my chest, and couldn't think of a single thing to say to it.
The doors opened on floor 5 with me still inside.

Imogen stepped out onto the brown lino. She looked down the corridor, past the baize board and the bowl-shaded bulbs and the doors with their enamel numbers, down a corridor longer than the building, which isn't on any drawing anyone has ever made, and then she turned round and smiled at me, kindly.
"Thank you, Ravi. I've wanted to see one of these with someone who isn't on the payroll."
